added_claim_errors: Step 2 tells the person to budget "roughly $1,240+" for the carryover-only case. That uses the $660 cap, and the 2026 figure is $680, so it should be about $1,220. Minor, and A also states $1,220-$1,240.
Run-out period "often ~90 days after year-end" is a typical figure, not a rule. It is unverified, but A frames it as common and tells the person to confirm.
The Proskauer link is the only source given. I could not open it, so I judged the $660 (2025) and $680 (2026) figures from my own knowledge of the IRS limits, and they are right.
"At most $660 of 2025 funds can move into 2026" puts the carryover in the wrong year. For the user's plan year ending Dec 31, 2026, the cap is $680, carrying into 2027.

"Grace period ... through March 15, 2026 ... against 2025 funds" and "does it run through March 15, 2026?" use the wrong year. The user's March dental work falls in March 2027, and March 15, 2026 has already passed.

"So at most $660 of your $1,900 survives on its own ... The March dental work does not get to spend the other $1,240" is wrong if the plan has a grace period. The grace period lets the whole balance pay for March work through March 15. B's step 1 then says the grace period "may qualify", which contradicts this.
The $1,240 forfeiture figure is built on the wrong $660 cap. The right carryover-case figure is $1,220.
The answer never tells the person to elect 2027 FSA money at open enrollment for the March work.

reasons: A corrects the premise at the start and uses the right year framing. It gives the carryover cap as $680 for 2026 (it also lists $660 for 2025), the grace period through March 15, and the forfeiture figure of $1,220-$1,240. It does not say everything is certainly lost, it tells the person to ask HR about carryover, grace period and run-out, and it warns against prepaying in December. It adds a correct HSA/FSA caution, and it only loosely touches the 2027 election point. B also corrects the premise and gives the same practical steps (move work to December, no prepaying, spend-down list). But it anchors everything to the wrong years: $660 of 2025 funds into 2026 and a March 15, 2026 grace end. It also flatly says the March dental work cannot use the other $1,240, which is wrong if the plan has a grace period, so its numbers and branches are unreliable.
